segs.text: How does a *nuclear submarine* actually work?
It can stay underwater for *months*, cross entire oceans without refueling, and never needs a breath of outside air.
Let's take one apart, piece by piece.
First, how does it even go down? Along the hull are *ballast tanks*.
On the surface they're full of *air*, so the sub floats like an empty bottle.
Open the vents on top, and *seawater* floods in from below. The air rushes out, the sub gets heavier, and it *sinks*.
Fins called *diving planes* tilt it down, like the wings of an airplane, while *trim tanks* fine-tune the balance.
Down here, there's no oxygen to burn. A *diesel engine* would choke in minutes.
US Navy subs can dive deeper than *240 meters*, where the water presses on every square meter of hull with about *240 tons*.
So the sub needs a power source that doesn't need air at all. That's the *reactor*.
Inside the reactor core are fuel rods, packed with *uranium*.
When a *neutron* hits a uranium-235 atom, the atom *splits* in two.
That split releases a burst of *energy*, and two or three new *neutrons*.
Those neutrons hit more atoms, which split and release more neutrons. A *chain reaction*.
And all that energy ends up as just one thing: *heat*.
To control it, the reactor uses *control rods*, made of materials that soak up neutrons.
Push them *in*, and the reaction slows down. Pull them *out*, and it speeds up.
In an emergency, they drop all the way in, and the reaction *stops* in seconds.
Here's the key idea: the reactor never touches the propeller. It only makes *heat*.
Water flows through the core and picks up that heat. This is the *primary loop*.
It gets hotter than *300 degrees Celsius*, but it never boils.
Why? A *pressurizer* keeps it under *high pressure*, over 150 times the air around you, so the water *can't boil*.
This water is *radioactive*, so it stays sealed in its own closed circuit, behind heavy *shielding*.
The hot water flows into the *steam generator*, through thousands of thin tubes.
Around those tubes is a second, separate loop of water, at *lower pressure*.
The *heat* crosses over. The *water* never does.
The second loop boils, and turns into high-pressure *steam*.
That steam blasts into the *turbines*, spinning their blades thousands of times a minute.
The *main engines* are turbines that drive the propeller.
Smaller *turbine generators* make *electricity* for everything else on board.
After the turbines, the used steam enters the *condenser*.
Cold *seawater*, pumped through tubes, cools it back into water.
Then it's pumped back to the steam generator, to boil all over again. A *closed loop*, with no exhaust.
Turbines spin far too fast for a propeller, so *reduction gears* slow the rotation down.
A long *shaft* carries that power through the back of the hull, to the *propeller*.
The blades throw *water back*, so the sub is pushed *forward*.
Many modern subs use a *pump-jet*, a propeller inside a duct, for an even quieter ride.
Now, the electricity. A submarine is basically a small *floating town*.
It makes *fresh water* by distilling seawater, boiling it and leaving the salt behind.
It makes *oxygen* by running electricity through water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen.
And *scrubbers* pull carbon dioxide out of the air, so the crew can breathe for months.
A submarine survives by staying *silent*.
Machinery sits on *rubber mounts*, and the hull is covered in sound-absorbing tiles.
It listens with *sonar*, hearing ships, whales, and other subs from miles away.
In new US subs, the *fuel* lasts the sub's entire life. More than *30 years*, without refueling.
So what limits how long it can stay down? Not the reactor. Not the air.
The limit is the *food*. About *three months*.
Time to go up. *High-pressure air* blasts into the ballast tanks.
The water is forced out, the sub gets *lighter*, and it rises back to the surface.
So: *uranium* makes *heat*. Heat makes *steam*. Steam spins *turbines*.
And turbines spin the *propeller*, and power a whole hidden world under the sea.
Follow for more of *how things work*.
